chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Crises of the 21st Century

lessons.title: 2008: How a US Housing Bust Became a Global Banking Crisis

body.text: Falling US house prices did not have to bring down the world's banks. What turned a housing loss into a global banking crisis was a system that had spread mortgage risk everywhere, funded it with overnight money, and left nobody able to see where the losses sat.

children.text: On 14 September 2007, a full year before Lehman Brothers failed, customers queued outside branches of Northern Rock, then the UK's fifth largest mortgage lender. About £1 billion was withdrawn in a single day, in Britain's first bank run in well over a century. Northern Rock had not made reckless loans to American subprime borrowers. Its problem was funding: it relied on borrowing from other institutions, and after the summer of 2007 they stopped lending. By February 2008, it had been nationalised.

This lesson is not about the housing bubble or the week Lehman fell. It is about the plumbing: how banks and shadow banks were wired together so that a US mortgage problem became a run on the global financial system.

stats.label: Estimated global writedowns
stats.context: IMF, April 2009; about two thirds borne by banks

body.caption: The 2008 crisis on the five-stage map

cells: Mortgages are bundled into securities, repackaged, rated highly and sold worldwide, funded heavily with short-term borrowing
US house prices fall and mortgage defaults rise, so the value of mortgage securities becomes uncertain
Lenders pull short-term funding from banks and shadow banks everywhere, from Northern Rock in 2007 to Lehman and AIG in 2008
Bank bailouts, guarantees, capital injections and central bank lending across the US, UK and Europe
New rules such as the Dodd-Frank Act and Basel III force banks to hold more capital and more stable funding

children.text: Build-up: The Securitisation Machine

Traditionally, a bank that gave you a home loan kept it on its books for 20 years, so it cared whether you could repay. By the 2000s, many lenders followed a different model: make the loan, then sell it on. The process of bundling loans and selling them as tradable securities is
securitisation

markDefs.definition: Pooling many loans, such as home loans, and selling securities backed by the payments on those loans to investors. The original lender gets cash immediately and passes the credit risk on to the buyers.

children.text: A mortgage broker or lender makes home loans, including to borrowers with weak credit histories.
The lender sells the loans to an investment bank and uses the cash to make more loans.
The investment bank pools thousands of loans into a
mortgage-backed security
and slices it into tranches with different levels of risk.

markDefs.definition: A bond whose interest and principal payments come from a pool of home loans. If borrowers default, the payments to the bond's holders shrink.

children.text: Riskier tranches are often pooled again into more complex securities, and many slices receive top credit ratings.
These securities are sold to banks, funds and insurers around the world, including in Germany, the UK and Iceland.

body.text: The model was called "originate to distribute". Every link in the chain was paid on volume at the moment a deal closed, while the risk of default was passed to someone further down the line. When no one in the chain keeps the risk, no one has a strong reason to check the loan.

body.title: Show me how tranches share out losses

children.text: Imagine a pool of home loans worth ₹100 crore, sliced into three tranches. Losses from defaults hit the lowest tranche first, then move upwards. This order is called the waterfall.

headers: Losses if the pool loses ₹10 crore

cells: ₹5 crore, a third of the tranche

children.text: The senior tranche looks extremely safe, because losses must exceed ₹20 crore, a fifth of the entire pool, before it loses a rupee. That logic earned many senior slices top ratings. But the models assumed defaults across different regions would not all rise together. When US house prices fell nationwide, they did.

body.title: Follow the Waterfall
body.prompt: Using the same ₹100 crore pool (senior ₹80 crore, mezzanine ₹15 crore, equity ₹5 crore), suppose defaults cause total losses of ₹12 crore. What percentage of the mezzanine tranche is lost? Give your answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: The equity tranche absorbs the first ₹5 crore and is wiped out. The remaining ₹7 crore of losses falls on the mezzanine tranche. ₹7 crore ÷ ₹15 crore × 100 = 46.7%. A pool loss of just 12% destroyed nearly half of a tranche that many investors had treated as moderately safe. Riskier slices repackaged into new securities could be wiped out entirely.

children.text: The Hidden Wiring: Shadow Banks and Repo
The securities were not just bought. They were bought with borrowed money, much of it borrowed overnight. Investment banks and other
shadow banks
funded huge portfolios in the
repo market

markDefs.definition: Financial firms that do bank-like things, such as borrowing short-term to fund long-term assets, without being regulated as banks or having access to deposit insurance and routine central bank support.

The market for repurchase agreements: short-term loans, often overnight, where a borrower sells securities to a lender and agrees to buy them back later at a slightly higher price. The securities act as collateral.

children.text: In a repo loan, the lender does not lend the full value of the collateral. It keeps a safety margin called a haircut. The borrower must fund the haircut with its own money.

body.caption: A higher haircut means the borrower must put in more of its own cash to hold the same securities.

body.title: A Run Without Queues
body.question: A shadow bank holds $100 million of mortgage-backed securities funded by overnight repo. The haircut is 2%, so it uses $2 million of its own money. After mortgage defaults rise, lenders raise the haircut to 20%. What must the shadow bank do the next morning?
options: Nothing, because the securities have not been sold
Find $18 million more of its own money, or sell securities it can no longer fund
Ask depositors for more deposits, which are insured
body.explanation: At a 20% haircut, holding $100 million of securities needs $20 million of its own money, not $2 million, so it must find $18 million more overnight. If it cannot, it must sell securities into a falling market, pushing prices down for everyone and raising haircuts further. Gorton and Metrick found that a repo haircut index rose from zero in early 2007 to nearly 50% in late 2008. That was a bank run, but by institutions, with no queues outside any branch.

body.title: A traditional bank run vs the 2007 to 2008 run

columns.label: Traditional bank run
points: Visible to everyone, as at Northern Rock
Deposit insurance and the central bank act as backstops
Regulators can see the bank's balance sheet

columns.label: Run on shadow banking
points: Institutional lenders refuse to roll over repo or raise haircuts
Invisible to the public until a firm suddenly fails
No deposit insurance and, at first, no automatic central bank access
Exposures spread across complex securities that were hard to value

children.text: How It Went Global

European banks were among the biggest buyers of US mortgage securities, and many funded them by borrowing dollars short-term. Other banks, like Northern Rock and Iceland's lenders, had no big subprime problem of their own but depended on the same wholesale funding markets that froze. The crisis travelled through balance sheets and funding markets, not through trade.

body.title: The run on the global banking system

events.title: Markets freeze
events.description: BNP Paribas suspends withdrawals from three funds exposed to US mortgage securities, saying it cannot value them. Interbank lending markets seize up.

events.title: Run on Northern Rock
events.description: About £1 billion is withdrawn in a day from a UK lender that relied on wholesale funding. It is nationalised in February 2008.

events.title: Bear Stearns is rescued
events.description: JPMorgan buys the US investment bank for about $10 a share, with the Fed funding $29 billion of its riskier assets.

events.title: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac taken over
events.description: The two giant US mortgage finance firms are placed into government conservatorship.

events.title: Lehman fails; AIG is rescued
events.description: Lehman Brothers files for bankruptcy. A day later, the Fed lends up to $85 billion to insurer AIG, which had sold protection on vast amounts of mortgage-linked securities, for a 79.9% stake.

events.title: Ireland guarantees its banks
events.description: After heavy outflows, Ireland guarantees virtually all liabilities of its main banks, a commitment of about €440 billion.

events.title: TARP becomes law
events.description: The US authorises up to $700 billion to stabilise its financial system.

events.title: Iceland's banks collapse
events.description: Landsbanki, Glitnir and Kaupthing are taken over in three days. Their combined debts were roughly ten times Iceland's GDP.

events.title: The UK's £500 billion package
events.description: Up to £50 billion of capital for banks, £200 billion of liquidity support and £250 billion of guarantees for bank borrowing.

events.title: Dodd-Frank Act signed
events.description: The biggest overhaul of US financial regulation since the 1930s becomes law.

body.text: Compare Iceland with India in 1991. Iceland's banks had borrowed abroad until they were about ten times the size of the economy, so no government could guarantee them. India's crisis was about a government running out of dollars; Iceland's was about banks that had grown too big for their own country to rescue.

children.text: Why Indian Banks Were Largely Spared

Indian markets fell sharply in 2008 and foreign money left, as you saw in Chapter 1. But Indian banks did not face a solvency crisis. They held very little of the complex US securities at the heart of the crisis, relied mainly on domestic deposits rather than wholesale funding, and had been restrained by the RBI during the boom years.

body.label: The RBI Leaned Against the Boom
body.value: 150% risk weight on commercial real estate loans
body.context: Under Governor Y.V. Reddy, between 2005 and 2007 the RBI raised risk weights on commercial real estate lending to 150% and lifted provisions on standard loans to personal borrowers, real estate and capital markets to 2%. Banks had to hold more capital and set aside more money precisely when those loans looked safest.

children.text: This is a countercyclical policy: tightening rules in a boom so that banks have more cushion when the bust comes. It was unfashionable at the time, because it slowed lending that looked profitable. After 2008, regulators worldwide adopted the same idea.

body.title: Name the Model
body.textWithBlank: The pre-2008 lending model, where lenders made loans only to sell them on to investors, was called originate to ___.
body.explanation: Originate to distribute. It separated the person making the lending decision from the person bearing the loss, which weakened lending standards across the chain.

children.text: Repair: The Rules Written After 2008
The Basel Committee, the body created after the Herstatt failure you met in Chapter 2, agreed a new rulebook called Basel III in December 2010. India began phasing it in from 1 April 2013.

body.caption: What Basel III changed, and the 2008 weakness each rule targets

cells: More common equity, the kind of capital that actually absorbs losses
Banks had too little real capital to absorb mortgage losses
Enough high-quality liquid assets to survive 30 days of stressed outflows
Firms like Northern Rock ran out of cash within days
Long-term assets funded with more stable, longer-term money
Long-term mortgage assets were funded with overnight repo
A cap on total exposure relative to capital, regardless of risk weights
Assets rated "safe" still carried huge losses
Extra capital built up during credit booms
Capital was thinnest exactly when the boom ended

body.title: Securitisation in India Today
body.scenario: An Indian NBFC that makes vehicle loans wants to raise money by selling a ₹500 crore pool of those loans to investors through pass-through certificates (PTCs), a form of securitisation. A friend says, "Isn't this exactly what caused 2008? India should ban it."
body.prompt: Explain how securitisation can be useful, what went wrong with it in 2008, and what safeguards would make you more comfortable investing in or lending to this NBFC.
body.modelAnswer: Securitisation is useful in itself. It lets an NBFC turn loans into cash so it can lend again, spreads risk to investors who want it, and can lower funding costs. What went wrong in 2008 was not the idea but how it was done: loans made purely to be sold, so lenders stopped caring about quality; layers of repackaging that made risk impossible to trace; ratings that assumed defaults would not rise together; and buyers who funded these securities with overnight borrowing. Safeguards to look for: first, the originator keeps some of the risk. RBI rules on securitisation require originators to retain a portion of the exposure, so the NBFC still loses money if its loans go bad. Second, a simple, transparent structure: one pool of vehicle loans with disclosed borrower data, not repackaged securities built on other securities. Third, credit enhancement, such as a cash reserve or subordinated tranche held by the NBFC, that absorbs the first losses. Fourth, a credible rating with clear stress test assumptions, including a scenario where defaults rise across the whole portfolio at once. Fifth, the NBFC itself should not depend on very short-term funding to survive, because that was how the 2008 losses turned into runs. Banning securitisation would throw away a useful tool. The lesson of 2008 is to keep incentives aligned and funding stable.

cards.definition: Pooling loans and selling securities backed by their payments, passing credit risk to investors.
A slice of a securitised pool with its own place in the loss waterfall, from senior (last to lose) to equity (first to lose).
A firm that borrows short to fund long-term assets like a bank, without bank regulation or deposit insurance.
The margin a repo lender keeps below the collateral's value. Higher haircuts force borrowers to put in more cash or sell.
Tightening rules during booms and easing them in busts, as the RBI did with real estate risk weights before 2008.
A Basel III rule requiring banks to hold enough liquid assets to survive 30 days of stressed outflows.

points: The 2008 crisis was a banking crisis: mortgage risk was securitised, repackaged and spread worldwide, then funded with short-term borrowing
The originate to distribute model weakened lending standards, and tranche ratings assumed defaults would not rise everywhere at once
The real panic was a run on shadow banking, as repo lenders raised haircuts from near zero to nearly 50% and forced fire sales
The crisis went global through funding markets and bank balance sheets, from Northern Rock in 2007 to Ireland's guarantee and Iceland's collapse in 2008
Indian banks were largely spared thanks to low exposure to toxic securities, deposit-based funding and the RBI's countercyclical tightening, and Basel III later made those lessons global rules
